title: Journal Sentiment Summary
summary: Combine entry selection, ordinary Java counting, and the learned mail service.

sources.title: Engineering Digest: Ultimate Guide to Scheduling Tasks with Cron Jobs in Spring Boot
Engineering Digest: Adding Sentiment to Journal App

richText: Digest operation
A journal digest counts sentiment labels already stored with entries.
It does not infer a sentiment from entry text.
A Spring service coordinates the operation: select one user’s entries, count their labels, then call the mail service.
The scheduled method controls when the service runs.
The mail service controls submission.
The count itself is ordinary Java.
A separate HTTP sentiment provider could assign labels when an entry is created.
That would use the client pattern from the external API lesson.
Reporting period and result
The query includes the user identity and one start-inclusive, end-exclusive interval.
Adjacent reporting periods then do not overlap.
A rolling seven-day interval and a calendar week are different choices.
A calendar week also needs a timezone and week boundary.
One run calculates its boundaries once.
Every entry selection in that run uses the same boundaries.
Entries without a label do not count.
Equal counts remain a tie unless the application defines a different rule.
Only users who opted in receive a digest.
An empty result reports that no labeled entries were found.

example.title: Count one period and submit its digest
description: Each tab names a file relative to the project root. Java `17` and Maven are required. `mvn spring-boot:run` starts this example after its external requirements are configured.
The tabs include `SentimentDigestService`, `DigestMailService`, SMTP settings, the application class, and the complete build file.
An SMTP provider with authenticated STARTTLS on port `587` must supply `MAIL_HOST`, `MAIL_USERNAME`, `MAIL_PASSWORD`, and an authorized `MAIL_FROM`.
The caller supplies entries, an authorized recipient, and the user’s stored consent.
The service is not exposed as a public endpoint.
For `user-42`, the input entries have labels `HAPPY`, `SAD`, and `HAPPY` inside the interval.
Entries from another user or outside the interval are ignored.
The caller supplies `start = Instant.parse("2026-10-05T00:00:00Z")` and `end = Instant.parse("2026-10-12T00:00:00Z")`.
This example receives entries as a `List<Entry>` argument.
explanation: Spring injects the mail service shown in the `DigestMailService.java` tab.
The application owns selection and counting.
The interval checks include the start and exclude the end.
The result reports every count, so a tie does not depend on map iteration order.
Mail submission happens only after counting.
The returned summary for the described input is shown below.
It is returned only if mail submission succeeds.

richText: A scheduled digest run
A real scheduled run first loads opted-in users.
It then loads each user’s entries for the fixed interval and calls the digest service.
The schedule from the previous lesson can trigger this work.
Persistence supplies the entries.
No new Spring annotation is needed for counting.
A job-and-user-and-period identifier can track pending, submitted, and failed digests.
In-memory completion state disappears on restart.
A submitted digest can still fail later delivery.
The mail lesson explains submission limits.
Kafka failure handling later explains durable publication and duplicate work.
